abstract: Abstract BRCA2 mutations contribute to the pathogenesis and treatment sensitivity of a subset of ovarian, breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancers. When these cancers become therapy resistant, secondary mutations that restore the BRCA2 open reading frame are found in half the cases, but other causes of resistance remain incompletely understood. Here, we identified translational readthrough of a premature termination codon (PTC) as a cause of resistance to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPis) and cisplatin in cells derived from the BRCA2 -mutated ovarian cancer line PEO1 by PARPi selection. Despite persistence of the signature 4965C > G (p.Y1655X) BRCA2 mutation, low-level expression of full-length BRCA2 protein was detectable in these cells by immunoblotting and tandem mass spectrometry. Either BRCA2 knockdown or gene interruption 5′ or 3′ to the PTC restored treatment sensitivity, implicating BRCA2 in the resistance. Reporter assays demonstrated UAG-selective readthrough in the resistant clones but not parental cells. Moreover, custom searching of global proteomic data indicated readthrough of stop codons, particularly UAGs, in additional proteins in the resistant clones. Finally, multi-omic analysis identified multiple changes in the nonsense-mediated decay and termination machineries that favor readthrough. Accordingly, the present results identify PTC readthrough as a potential mechanism of drug resistance in cells with BRCA2 nonsense mutations.
methods:
Materials and methods
Reagents
Pamiparib was a kind gift from X. Wang (Beigene, Beijing, China). Sources of all commercially available reagents are listed in
Supplementary Table S1
.
Biological resources
PEO1 and PEO4 cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Minimal Essential Medium (DMEM) with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum, 40 μM nonessential amino acids, 10 μg/mL insulin, 40 units/mL penicillin G, 40 μg/mL streptomycin, and 2 mM glutamine (Medium A) at 37°C in an atmosphere containing 5% (v/v) CO
2
. ABT
R
clones were derived by culturing PEO1 cells in increasing concentrations of veliparib, starting with 5 μM, over a 6-month period and then cloned using cloning rings. Identity of lines and clones was confirmed by short tandem repeat profiling and by sequencing that confirmed the presence of pathognomonic
BRCA2
mutation. Prior to each experiment, ABT
R
clones were removed from veliparib for at least 3 days.
As described in the Supplementary data, targeted gene interruptions were performed using previously reported CRISPR/Cas9 methods [
38
,
58
] along with sgRNAs listed in
Supplementary Table S1
. Stable transfectants were selected in 3 μg/ml puromycin and cloned by limiting dilution before characterization. Transient knockdowns were performed by electroporation using the siRNAs listed in
Supplementary Table S1
and previously reported methods [
38
,
58
] described in the Supplementary data. Cells were assayed for drug sensitivity, DNA damage-induced formation of RAD51 foci, mRNA levels, or protein expression 48 h after siRNA transfection.
Colony formation assay
Aliquots containing 750–1000 cells were plated in medium A, allowed to adhere for 4 h (transfected cells) or 14–18 h (untransfected cells), and treated for 48 h with diluent [0.1% v/v dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)] or the indicated drug. At the completion of the incubation, cells were washed in serum-free DMEM and incubated in drug-free medium A for 10–14 days before staining.
Cell fractionation and immunoblotting
Nuclear lysates were prepared using the NE-PER kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific #78833). Alternatively, cells were lysed in 6 M guanidine hydrochloride containing 100 mM Tris–HCl (pH 8.5 at 21°C), 10 mM ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid, 1% (v/v) 2-mercaptoethanol, and 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF). After treatment as described in the Supplementary data, aliquots containing 50 μg of total cellular protein or 20 μg of nuclear protein were subjected to sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE), transferred to nitrocellulose, and probed with antibodies listed in
Supplementary Table S1
.
HR and nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) NHEJ assays
HR was assessed using the DR-GFP plasmid as previously described [
59
] using pCherry as a transfection control. HR results are presented as the ratio of the number of EGFP
+
mCherry
+
double-positive cells to the total number of mCherry
+
cells. Results in each line or clone were subsequently normalized to the value for PEO1 cells, which was set at 1.0. NHEJ was assessed using the pEGFP-Pem1-Ad2 plasmid as described [
60
].
mRNA Sequencing
PEO1 (no treatment) and ABT
R
clones growing stably in 40 μM veliparib were harvested in biological triplicates for mRNA sequencing. RNA was purified using a Qiagen AllPrep DNA/RNA mini kit. PolyA
+
mRNA was purified using oligo-dT attached to magnetic beads and converted to complementary DNA (cDNA) with the TruSeq RNA sample prep kit v2 (Illumina). cDNAs were denatured, enriched by PCR, and analyzed on an Illumina HiSeq 2000 using TruSeq SBS sequencing kit (version 3) and HCS software (v2.0.12). Bioinformatic analysis and confirmatory quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) or PCR assays are described in the
Supplementary Methods and
Supplementary Tables S1
and
S6
.
BROCA analysis and whole exome sequencing
Targeted capture and massively parallel sequencing of DNA repair genes (BROCA) was performed using the gene panel previously described [
61
]. Read depth at
BRCA2
c.4965 was 128 to 204 reads in the four ABT
R
clones. Whole exome sequencing was performed and analyzed as recently described [
62
].
Readthrough assays
A readthrough reporter plasmid was constructed by amplifying wt
BRCA2
nucleotides 4663–5991 (encoding amino acids 1555–1997) from OVCAR8 cells into KpnI/EagI-cut pEFXS, which has FLAG and S peptide tags N-terminal and C-terminal to the insert, respectively. The 4965C > G, 4965C > A, or 4964A > G/4965C > A mutations were inserted by site-directed mutagenesis. After the plasmid was transfected by electroporation, cells were incubated for 48 h in medium A in the absence or presence of 400 ng/ml G418 for the last 24 h. After cell lysates were prepared in RIPA buffer, S peptide-tagged proteins were pulled down using anti-FLAG M2-agarose or S protein-agarose and probed for the presence of S peptide-containing products.
Mass spectrometry
Methods for the MS/MS analysis of BRCA2 immunoprecipitates and the readthrough construct, as well as untargeted LC-MS/MS analysis of parental PEO1 cells and ABT
R
clones, are described in the Supplementary data. The untargeted LC-MS/MS data were searched for readthrough peptides using Sequester search engine in Proteome Discoverer 2.5 suite against the UniProt human database containing additional BRCA2 protein sequences in which the Y1655 residue was replaced individually by each of the other 19 amino acids or a stop codon. The search parameters are described in the Supplementary data. Peptides used in confirmatory parallel reaction monitoring are listed in
Supplementary Table S5
.
Bioinformatic and statistical analyses
Bioinformatic analyses were performed using publicly available programs as described in the Supplementary data. Statistical analyses of biological experiments, excluding proteomics and RNA sequencing, were performed using GraphPad Prism version 10.2.1.

Introduction
Genetic or epigenetic modifications that disable the homologous recombination (HR) DNA repair pathway are present in a subset of ovarian, breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancers [
1–5
]. Although alterations in a variety of HR genes are detected, deleterious mutations in
BRCA1
and
BRCA2
are most common. Building on preclinical observations of synthetic lethality between
BRCA1
or
BRCA2
(
BRCA1/2
) mutations and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPis) [
6
,
7
], clinical studies have shown that PARPis are active as monotherapy in advanced disease or as maintenance therapy in these cancers [
5
,
8–11
]. For example, up to 50% of high-grade serous ovarian cancers (HGSOCs), the most common and deadliest subtype, harbor genetic or epigenetic alterations affecting HR [
2
,
12
,
13
]; and many of these HGSOCs harboring HR alterations respond to PARPis administered as monotherapy [
14
] or as maintenance therapy after second- or third-line platinum-containing salvage regimens [
15
,
16
]. Moreover, when given as maintenance therapy after first-line treatment, PARPis induce even greater improvements in progression-free and overall survival of
BRCA1
/
2
-mutated ovarian cancer [
17–19
]. Even in this setting, however, >50% of ovarian cancers relapse, reflecting the development of PARPi-resistant disease [
10
,
18–21
]. PARPi-resistant disease likewise develops in a majority of patients receiving PARPi treatment for
BRCA1/2
-mutated prostate [
22–24
] or pancreatic cancer [
25
].
Several mechanisms of PARPi resistance have been previously identified [
10
,
11
,
26–29
]. In cases where
BRCA1/2
variants confer PARPi sensitivity, secondary mutations that restore complete or partial HR function, including reversion to wild-type (WT) sequence, amino acid substitutions, alterations in splice sites, and large and small indels that restore the open reading frame, can sometimes be detected as PARPi resistance develops [
14
,
30–32
]. In the face of selection, alternative splicing can also result in restoration of functional BRCA1 or BRCA2 protein in the presence of a nonsense mutation [
33
,
34
]. In other instances, HR can be restored by alterations in alternative repair pathways. For example, loss of 53BP1, RIF1, or components of the shieldin complex can enhance HR and cause PARPi resistance in
BRCA1
-mutated cells [
35–38
]. Moreover, changes to PARP1 itself, including downregulation to decrease drug-induced trapping [
39
], phosphorylation to increase activity [
40
], or point mutations that alter drug binding [
41
], can confer PARPi resistance. Finally, efflux by drug exporters can contribute to resistance to some PARPis [
42
].
In cells with
BRCA1
or
BRCA2
nonsense mutations, translational readthrough could in principle also restore expression of these tumor suppressor proteins. Under ordinary conditions, the stop codons UAG, UAA, and UGA are recognized by eukaryotic termination factor 1 (ETF1), which activates GTP hydrolysis by its binding partner ETF3, leading to conformational change in the complex that facilitates ETF1-catalyzed hydrolysis of the covalent bond between the nascent peptide chain and tRNA in the peptidyl site of the ribosome [
43
,
44
]. This termination process is estimated to be 99.9% accurate at natural stop codons [
45
,
46
] and is influenced by a number of factors, which include the identity of the nucleotides 3′ to the termination codon [
47
] as well as levels of ETF1 [
48
,
49
], the ATP-dependent RNA helicase DDX19 [
50
,
51
], elongation factor eEF1A [
52
,
53
], and tRNAs able to compete for binding to the stop codon [
54
]. To further diminish inadvertent stop codon readthrough, messenger RNAs (mRNAs) with nonsense mutations are also subject to nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), a process that causes preferential degradation of faulty mRNA transcripts with premature termination codons (PTCs), splice site alterations, or other abnormalities [
50
,
55
,
56
].
Here we identify PTC readthrough as the main mechanism of BRCA2 restoration in a series of PARPi-resistant clones derived from the ovarian cancer cell line PEO1, which harbors a
BRCA2
nonsense mutation [
57
]. Despite the absence of detectable secondary
BRCA2
mutations or alternative splicing, the resistant PEO1 cells express low levels of BRCA2 protein that reflect increased BRCA2 mRNA and enhanced codon-specific readthrough. To our knowledge, this is the first report of PTC readthrough as a mechanism of acquired drug resistance in cancer.

Results
Characterization of PARPi-resistant clones
Starting with the platinum- and PARPi-sensitive HGSOC cell line PEO1, which is HR deficient due to a homozygous nonsense mutation [
57
] at codon 1655 of the
BRCA2
open reading frame (denoted 4965C > G herein), PARPi-resistant cells were derived by continuous treatment with increasing concentrations of the PARPi veliparib (ABT-888). Once cells had been repeatedly expanded in 40 μM veliparib, multiple clones designated ABT
R
(for ABT888 resistant) were isolated (Fig.
1A
). Two (ABT
R
2 and ABT
R
3) were arbitrarily chosen for mechanistic studies, with key experiments validated in the other two clones. PEO4 cells, which come from the same patient as PEO1 cells but contain a secondary mutation in
BRCA2
(c.4965C > T) that eliminates the nonsense mutation and restores the WT codon [
57
], served as a control in some experiments.
Figure 1.
Isolation and characterization of PARPi-resistant PEO1 clones. (
A
), strategy for isolating PARPi-resistant (ABT
R
) clones. (
B
), cross-resistance of veliparib-selected clones to multiple PARPis. The indicated cells were treated for 48 h with veliparib, olaparib, or rucaparib, washed, and allowed to form colonies under drug-free conditions. Results are expressed as the percentage of colonies formed in cells treated with diluent (0.1% DMSO). Error bars, ± SD of triplicate aliquots. Results in each panel are representative of 3–10 independent biological replicates. (
C
), quantification of γH2AX foci (top) or RAD51 foci (bottom) 6 h after treatment with 10 Gy ionizing radiation or addition of 20 μM veliparib. Nuclei (100/slide) were scored manually after each treatment. Error bars in panel (C) represent the mean ± SEM of three independent experiments. (
D
), HR activity assayed using a transient transfection of DR-GFP plasmid [
59
] in cells exposed to diluent or 20 μM veliparib for 48 h. In each assay, HR activity of PEO1 cells was set to 1. Error bars, ± SEM of four independent assays. (
E
), heat map showing DNA repair genes (GO: 0006281) significantly changed between parental PEO1 cells and clones ABT
R
1, ABT
R
2, ABT
R
3, or ABT
R
4 [|log
2
FC| > 1, false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05].
BRCA2
is indicated as one of the top differentially expressed genes. Inset, Sanger sequencing profile of PEO4, PEO1, and the ABT
R
clones in the region of the truncating
BRCA2
mutation that is pathognomonic of PEO1 cells [
57
].
In colony-forming assays the ABT
R
clones were resistant to veliparib (Fig.
1B
) and to the PARPis olaparib, rucaparib, niraparib, and pamiparib (Fig.
1B
and
Supplementary Fig. S1A
and
B
), indicating broad PARPi resistance rather than a mechanism specific to veliparib. In addition, the ABT
R
clones were cross-resistant to cisplatin and doxorubicin, which damage DNA directly (
Supplementary Fig. S1C
and D), but not to agents with other mechanisms of action such as gemcitabine or paclitaxel (
Supplementary Fig. S1E
and F).
To begin to identify the resistance mechanism, we examined the induction of DNA damage and repair. After treatment with either PARPi or ionizing irradiation (IR), γH2AX foci formed (Fig.
1C
,upper panel and
Supplementary Fig. S2A
), confirming that DNA damage was occurring in the ABT
R
clones during PARPi exposure, as has previously been reported in both HR-proficient and HR-deficient cells [
7
]. These results, which reflect the continued ability of PARPi to inhibit poly(ADP-ribosylation) in these clones (
Supplementary Fig. S2B
), argued against decreased PARPi accumulation or diminished PARP inhibition as major contributors to the resistance.
In contrast to parental PEO1 cells, the ABT
R
clones formed RAD51 foci after PARPi or IR exposure (Fig.
1C
,lower panel and
Supplementary Fig. S2A
), indicating restoration of RAD51 recruitment to sites of DNA damage. Assays using the DR-GFP reporter plasmid [
59
] likewise confirmed restoration of HR repair (Fig.
1D
). Moreover, despite a lack of identifiable deficiency in any NHEJ protein examined (
Supplementary Fig. S2C
), PARPi-induced activation of NHEJ was diminished in the ABT
R
clones relative to PEO1 cells (
Supplementary Fig. S2D
).
To search for a potential explanation for HR restoration in the ABT
R
clones, mRNA sequencing was performed. Examination of transcripts with gene ontology annotations of “DNA repair” indicated that multiple genes were differentially expressed in the resistant clones (Fig.
1E
). Surprisingly,
BRCA2
was among the transcripts most strongly upregulated relative to the parental PEO1 cells (Fig.
1E
).
Because secondary
BRCA2
mutations have been reported in cisplatin-selected PEO1 cells [
57
], the
BRCA2
locus was examined by three methods: Sanger sequencing in the region of the
BRCA2
PTC, targeted capture followed by massively parallel sequencing of full-length
BRCA2
and other HR genes [
61
] with a read depth of 128–204 reads across codon 1655 in the four ABT
R
clones, and whole exome sequencing. By all methods, the 4965C > G mutation was present without WT reads (Fig.
1E
,right panel and
Supplementary Fig. S3A
), and no secondary mutations or copy number changes were identified in
BRCA2
or any other DNA repair gene. BRCA2 mRNA likewise contained the 4965C > G mutation (
Supplementary Fig. S3B
).
In line with the idea that PARPi-induced killing reflects trapping of PARP1 and PARP2 at sites of DNA damage, PARPi resistance has been observed in cells with diminished PARP1 or PARP2 expression [
63–65
]. Immunoblotting, however, revealed that PARP1 and PARP2, as well as the PARP1 binding partner HPF-1, increased rather than decreased in the resistant clones relative to PEO1 (
Supplementary Fig. S2C
). RAD51 was also upregulated at the mRNA and protein levels in the ABT
R
clones (
Supplementary Fig. S2E
).
BRCA2 dependence of PARPi resistance in ABT
R
clones
In further studies, siRNA-mediated RAD51 knockdown sensitized the ABT
R
clones to veliparib (Fig.
2A
and
Supplementary Fig. S4A
) as well as rucaparib and cisplatin (
Supplementary Fig. S4B
), confirming a critical role for RAD51 in the resistance. Knockdown of RAD52, a protein implicated in HR when the classical RAD51 loading pathway is inactive [
66
], had no impact on PARPi sensitivity in the ABT
R
clones (Fig.
2B
and
Supplementary Fig. S4C
) even though RAD52 was overexpressed, albeit to varying degrees, in the resistant clones. In contrast, knockdown of PALB2 (Fig.
2C
) or BRCA1 (
Supplementary Fig. S4D
), like RAD51 knockdown, restored PARPi sensitivity of resistant clones that were tested. Moreover, BRCA2 knockdown resulted in diminished formation of DNA damage-induced RAD51 foci (Fig. 2D and
Supplementary Fig. S4E
) as well as diminished resistance to PARPis and cisplatin (Fig.
2E
and
Supplementary Fig. S4E
and
F
), suggesting that RAD51 might be recruited to sites of DNA damage by the classical BRCA1-PALB2-BRCA2 pathway [
67
].
Figure 2.
Role of BRCA2 in PARPi resistance of the ABT
R
clones. Parental PEO1 cells or the clones ABT
R
2 and ABT
R
3 were transfected with siRNAs to RAD51 (
A
), RAD52 (
B
), PALB2 (
C
), or BRCA2 (
D
,
E
) or nontargeting siRNA (siControl) and incubated for 48 h. Cells were then treated with 10 Gy IR and examined 6 h later for RAD51 foci (D) or treated with veliparib for 48 h and allowed to form colonies in the absence of drug (A–C, E). Sequences targeted by BRCA2 siRNAs are indicated in the schematic at the top of panel (D). Insets in panels (A–C) confirm knockdowns by immunoblotting of nuclei (A, B) or whole cell lysates (C) with LMNB1 and RAF1 as loading controls or by qRT-PCR (E) with GAPDH as a control. Dashed line in panel (B) inset indicates a longer exposure from the same experiment in lanes 1–3 than in lanes 4–9. Error bars in panels (A–C) and (E) represent ± SD of triplicate plates. Each panel is representative of 3–5 independent experiments with the same siRNAs. Error bars in panel (D) and inset (E) represent the mean ± SEM from three independent siRNA transfections.
To further investigate the unexpected observation that BRCA2 knockdown sensitized the resistant clones to PARPis despite the presence of the exon 11 stop codon (Fig.
1E
and
Supplementary Fig. S3
), we probed nuclear lysates for BRCA2 protein using multiple reagents. A rabbit polyclonal serum raised against a peptide containing BRCA2 aa 450–500 revealed increased expression of a presumptive BRCA2 truncated protein product [
68
] at ∼250 kD in the ABT
R
clones compared to PEO1 cells (Fig.
3A
). Upon prolonged exposure, a fainter band comigrating with full-length BRCA2 in PEO4 cells was also detected in the ABT
R
clones (Fig.
3A
,arrowhead). Moreover, a rabbit monoclonal antibody recognizing an epitope near the C-terminus of BRCA2 and a murine monoclonal antibody detecting an epitope just C-terminal to the stop codon consistently reacted with a band in the resistant clones that migrated with full-length BRCA2 (Fig.
3B
and C). Compared to Ovcar8 or COV362 cells, which harbor WT BRCA2, the signal detected at the molecular weight of full-length BRCA2 was ∼2-fold lower in PEO4 cells and 8- to 16-fold lower in ABT
R
clones (
Supplementary Fig. S5A
). The species that comigrated with full-length BRCA2 protein, along with some of the smaller species detected by the N- and C-terminal antibodies, were diminished by BRCA2 siRNA (Fig. 3D and
Supplementary Fig. S5B and C
). In addition, after pulldown with the antiserum recognizing the BRCA2 N-terminal region, the protein that comigrated with full-length BRCA2 was detected with the C-terminal antibody (Fig.
3E
).
Figure 3.
Expression of BRCA2 in ABT
R
cells. Nuclei prepared from the indicated cells were subjected to SDS–PAGE and immunoblotting with a polyclonal antiserum raised against a peptide in the N-terminal quarter of BRCA2 (
A
), a monoclonal rabbit antibody that recognizes an epitope near the BRCA2 C-terminus (
B
), or a mouse monoclonal antibody that recognizes an epitope just distal to the Y1655* premature termination site (
C
). Locations of immunizing peptides are shown in diagram below panel (A) and specified in
Supplementary Table S1
. Dashed line in panel (A) indicates removal of four intervening lanes from each single exposure. (
D
), 48 h after the indicated cells were transfected with control siRNA or the BRCA2 siRNAs shown in Fig.
2D
, nuclei were isolated and subjected to immunoblotting. (
E
), lysates prepared from the indicated cells using RIPA buffer were subjected to immunoprecipitation with BRCA2 N-terminal antiserum #1 followed by immunoblotting with the indicated antibody. (
F
), after immunoprecipitation of BRCA2 from PEO4, ABT
R
2, or ABT
R
3 cells, tryptic digests were subjected to LC/MS/MS. BRCA2 peptides identified in this analysis (
Supplementary Table S4
) are indicated with vertical green bars. Blue horizontal bar indicates site of antibody binding. PEO1 cells or the indicated ABT
R
2 clones derived after transfection with Cas9 and nontargeting sgRNA or sgRNA targeting BRCA2 nt 5670–5689 (
G
) or 1380–1399 (
H
) were treated for 48 h with veliparib, washed, and allowed to form colonies. Insets, nuclear lysates were subjected to immunoblotting with the indicated antibodies. Arrowheads in panels (A–E), (G), and (H) indicate polypeptides that co-migrate with full-length BRCA2 in
BRCA2
wt Ovcar8 cells as shown in
Supplementary Fig. S5A
.
To better characterize the BRCA2 species present, BRCA2 immunoprecipitated from the ABT
R
clones and from PEO4 cells using the N-terminal anti-BRCA2 antibodies was subjected to tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS). This analysis identified five BRCA2 peptides N-terminal to the stop codon in ABT
R
2 cells and four BRCA2 peptides C-terminal to the stop codon, including a peptide at aa 3371–3381 near the distal C terminus (Fig.
3F
). BRCA2 peptides C-terminal to the stop codon were detected by MS/MS in BRCA2 immunoprecipitates from the other three ABT
R
clones as well (Fig.
3F
,
Supplementary Fig. S5D
, and
Supplementary Table S4
).
To assess whether the putative BRCA2 full-length protein reflects low-level presence of a subclone with a secondary
BRCA2
mutation similar to PEO4 cells despite failure to detect a secondary mutation by sequencing, the four ABT
R
clones were subcloned. All subclones contained a protein that reacted with the C-terminal antibody and migrated with full-length BRCA2 (
Supplementary Fig. S5E
).
To distinguish the relative contributions of the putative full-length BRCA2 protein versus the more abundantly expressed N-terminal fragment (Fig.
3A
) to PARPi resistance, the
BRCA2
gene in ABT
R
2 cells was interrupted 3′ to the nonsense mutation, resulting in two subclones. One (clone ΔC1) was sensitized to PARPi (Fig.
3G
) and cisplatin (
Supplementary Fig. S5F
), whereas the other (clone ΔC2) was not. Immunoblotting demonstrated loss of full-length BRCA2 in the clone that was sensitized, whereas low levels of full-length BRCA2 were still detected in the clone that was not (inset, Fig.
3G
). In further experiments, the BRCA2 gene was also interrupted 5′ to the
BRCA2
nonsense mutation. This genomic alteration also abolished expression of the full-length BRCA2 protein and restored PARPi sensitivity in the single knockout clone recovered (clone ΔN1, Fig.
3H
).
ABT
R
clones harbor multiple alterations in RNA metabolism pathways
Having established that BRCA2 plays a critical role in the PARPi resistance, we examined potential explanations for its re-expression. Although PTCs in
BRCA1
exon 11 as well as
BRCA2
exon 12 can be bypassed by alternative splicing, neither PCR-based assessment nor Sanger sequencing of the entire BRCA2 cDNA from ABT
R
2 or ABT
R
3 cells (see Supplementary data) provided evidence of alternative splicing.
Because messages with PTCs are often downregulated by NMD [
69–71
], the elevated BRCA2 message (Figs
1E
and
4A
) raised the possibility that NMD might be altered in the ABT
R
clones. To further assess this possibility, we examined the relative expression of mRNAs encoded by 31 genes with PTCs in the parental PEO1 cells that had mRNA expression in ABT
R
2 cells. Of these 31 genes, only 14 showed a >2-fold change in ABT
R
2 cells relative to PEO1 (Fig.
4B
), possibly reflecting fact that NMD is more prominent when PTCs are located close to splice junctions or the poly(A) tail [
69–71
]. Of these 14 differentially expressed genes, 12 were upregulated ≥2-fold and two were downregulated ≥2-fold (
P
= .06 by Bernard’s test), indicating a trend toward upregulation of transcripts with PTCs in the ABT
R
2 clone relative to parental PEO1 cells. Similar results were observed in ABT
R
3 cells (
Supplementary Fig. S6A
).

Examination of the RNAseq data revealed diminished levels of several transcripts encoding proteins involved in RNA metabolism, including NMD pathways, in the ABT
R

4C
and
Supplementary Fig. S6B

71

R

Supplementary Fig. S7

4D

and
Supplementary Fig. S6B

Looking more broadly, we also examined proteins involved in mRNA translation. Downregulation of ETF1, the protein responsible for recognizing all three native stop codons in human cells [
72
], was observed at the mRNA and protein levels (Fig.
4E
and
Supplementary Fig. S6B

Supplementary Fig. S6C
), giving rise to higher total EEF1A protein (Fig.

48
,
49
,
52
,
53
]. Thus, ABT
R

Increased codon-specific nonsense codon readthrough in the ABT
R
clones
In further experiments, the ability of ABT
R
clones to read through the
BRCA2
PTC was examined using a construct that contained
BRCA2
nucleotides 4663–5991 (straddling the PTC at nucleotides 4965–4967) with cDNA encoding FLAG and S peptide tags at the 5′ and 3′ ends (Fig.
5A
, schematic). IP with anti-FLAG antibody and blotting with antibody to S peptide demonstrated readthrough of the truncated plasmid in the ABT
R
clones but not parental PEO1 cells (Fig.
5A
, second panel and
Supplementary Fig. S8A
). G418, an aminoglycoside known to induce termination codon readthrough [
73
,
74
], provided a positive control for readthrough in the PEO1 cells (Fig.
5A
and
Supplementary Fig. S8A
, third panel).

When protein encoded by the PTC-containing reporter construct was immunoprecipitated from ABT
R
2 cells and analyzed by MS/MS-based sequencing, 23 peptides were readily detected (Fig.
5B
). Analysis of the peptide encoded by the sequence containing the PTC indicated that tyrosine had been incorporated where UAG would have resulted in termination of translation (Fig.
5B
). Insertion of tyrosine at this position was also observed in the other three clones (
Supplementary Fig. S8B–D
). A separate targeted parallel reaction monitoring experiment also confirmed incorporation of tyrosine at this position (
Supplementary Fig. S9
). Interestingly, replacement of TAG in the reporter construct with the other two stop codons, TAA or TGA, markedly diminished readthrough in ABT
R
clones unless G418 was added (Fig.
5C
and
Supplementary Fig. S8E
), suggesting selective UAG readthrough.
To identify possible readthrough of other stop codons in the ABT
R
clones, we searched the proteomic data (
Supplementary Fig. S7
) for tryptic peptides encoded by sequences 3′ to naturally occurring termination codons. This analysis identified 53 peptides from 49 proteins that were consistent with readthrough of naturally occurring stop codons (
Supplementary Table S2A
and
Supplementary Fig. S10
). Comparison of the ABT
R
cells with parental PEO1 cells indicated that five of these peptides decreased and 19 increased >2-fold (Fig.
5D
), suggesting a propensity toward upregulation in the resistant cells (χ
2
= 4.46,
P
= .035). Further examination indicated that 17 of these 19 increases occurred in proteins with natural UAG stop codons (upper inset, Fig.
5D
) even though the expected frequency of UAG codons is 22% in the human genome. This indicates a skewing of readthrough events (χ
2
= 18,
P
= 2.2 × 10
−5
) that is consistent with the UAG preference shown in Fig.
5C
and
Supplementary Fig. S8
. Among the 17 peptides reflecting >2-fold increases in readthrough events at UAGs, 12 were peptides spanning the naturally occurring stop codons, and 11 of the 12 peptides contained Tyr at the site of the stop codon (lower inset, Fig.
5D
;
Supplementary Table S2A
). The presence of a subset of these readthrough peptides was confirmed by comparison of the MS/MS spectra from the cell lysates to synthetic peptides with the identified sequence (
Supplementary Fig. S10
). Although these results raised the possibility of a mutation in a tyrosine tRNA so that it could recognize UAG, tRNA sequencing failed to identify any change in the sequence (not shown) or abundance (
Supplementary Fig. S6E
) of the 14 tyrosine tRNAs present in these cells. Likewise, tRNA mass spectrometry failed to identify a tRNA modification common to all four clones that could readily explain the readthrough (
Supplementary Table S3
).
To further confirm increased readthrough in the ABT
R
cells, we performed immunoblotting for PSMA4, U2AF2, and ASRGL1, the three proteins in which the readthrough products were predicted to have the largest change in molecular weight (
Supplementary Table S2B
). In all cases, immunoblotting indicated a distinct protein species slightly larger than the full-length protein in the ABT
R
clones but not PEO1 or PEO4 cells (Fig.
5E
), providing further support for the presence of translational readthrough.
Discussion
Previous studies identified restoration of HR as a major cause of PARPi and platinum resistance in
BRCA1/2
-mutated ovarian cancer [
26
,
75
]. A number of mechanisms of HR restoration have previously been described, including secondary mutations that restore the open reading frame [
14
,
30
,
31
], alternative splicing [
33
], exon skipping [
34
], and downregulation of 53BP1 or other components of the shieldin complex [
35–38
]. The present study suggests that HR can also be restored through translational readthrough.
Several observations indicate that full-length BRCA2 is expressed in the ABT
R
clones despite the presence of a PTC at codon 1655. First, multiple antibodies directed against different epitopes, including an epitope near the C-terminus of the protein, recognize a polypeptide in all four ABT
R
clones that co-migrates with BRCA2 from PEO4 cells (Fig.
3A
–
C
and
Supplementary Fig. S5A
). Importantly, the putative full-length species recognized by these antibodies is downregulated by BRCA2 siRNAs (Fig.
3
D and
Supplementary Fig. S5B
and C), providing further assurance that BRCA2 is being detected. Second, tandem mass spectrometry of BRCA2 immunoprecipitated from each of the clones identified multiple peptides distal to the PTC, including a peptide very close to the C-terminus in ABT
R
2 (Fig.
3F
and
Supplementary Fig. S5D
).
Additional results support the view that this full-length BRCA2 contributes to resistance. First, assays for RAD51 foci and repair of the DR-GFP reporter construct indicate that HR has been restored in the ABT
R
clones (Fig.
1C
and D). Second, the resistant clones are sensitized by RAD51 knockdown (Fig.
2A
and
Supplementary Fig. S4A
), indicating the critical role of HR in the resistance. Third, knockdown of BRCA1, PALB2, or BRCA2 also restores PARPi sensitivity (Fig.
2
and
Supplementary Fig. S4
), which suggests that RAD51 has been loaded through the canonical BRCA2-dependent pathway. Finally, interruption of the
BRCA2
gene either 3′ or 5′ to the PTC also sensitizes ABT
R
cells (Fig.
3G
and H), suggesting that full-length BRCA2 rather than any fragment observed in this study is responsible for the resistance. While the levels of full-length BRCA2 are substantially lower than those observed in PEO4 cells (Fig.
3A
–
C
and
Supplementary Fig. S5A
), the observation that low levels of BRCA2 are sufficient to contribute to resistance is reminiscent of an earlier report that very low levels of XPB and XPD generated through aminoglycoside-induced readthrough can confer resistance to UV irradiation [
76
].
Several additional observations provide evidence that the observed BRCA2 re-expression results from PTC readthrough. First, deep sequencing failed to show evidence for a small contaminating population of cells lacking the PTC (
Supplementary Fig. S3A
). Second, subcloning of the ABT
R
cells resulted in subclones that uniformly expressed low levels of full-length BRCA2 protein just like the initial clones (
Supplementary Fig. S5E
). Third, our studies failed to show evidence for alternative splicing. These observations argue against the most likely alternative explanations. Accordingly, we considered the possibility that resistant clones were able to read through the UAG stop codon, whereas the parental PEO1 cells were not. Consistent with this hypothesis, readthrough was observed in all four ABT
R
clones using a reporter that contained 1326 bp of natural BRCA2 cDNA surrounding the PTC (Fig.
5A
and
Supplementary Fig. S8A
). Importantly, readthrough of the same construct was not observed in parental PEO1 cells except in the presence of G418, an agent known to cause readthrough [
73
,
74
,
77
].
While BRCA2 restoration contributes to the resistance, it is possible that RAD51 overexpression also contributes. In particular, the ∼2-fold increase in RAD51 mRNA and protein in the ABT
R
clones (Fig.
3D
and
Supplementary Fig. S2E
) might facilitate recombinase loading by the small amount of full-length BRCA2 protein present in the ABT
R
cells. Importantly, however,
BRCA2
gene interruption 3′ to the PTC sensitized the ABT
R
2 cells without detectable RAD51 downregulation (
Supplementary Fig. S5F
), arguing that BRCA2 is playing a major role in resistance independent of any role of RAD51 upregulation.
Although the BRCA2 readthrough resulted in a readily detectable phenotype, stop codon readthrough was not limited to BRCA2. Global proteomic analysis utilizing a customized searching strategy identified 49 proteins in which tryptic peptides encoded by sequences 3′ to naturally occurring stop codons were detectable in ABT
R
cells (Fig.
5D
). For 40 of the 49 proteins, the amount of readthrough was elevated in ABT
R
clones relative to parental PEO1 cells (
Supplementary Table S2A
). In accordance with these results, Western blotting identified species slightly larger than full-length protein in the ABT
R
clones but not PEO1 cells (Fig.
5E
). Interestingly, further analysis indicated that readthrough of naturally occurring stop codons also occurred predominantly at UAG with minimal occurrence at other stop codons (Fig.
5D
and
Supplementary Table S2A
).
Although the present study establishes translational readthrough as a likely contributor to PARPi and platinum resistance in PEO1 cells, it also leaves a number of questions unanswered. First, the cause of the translational readthrough in the ABT
R
clones, like the mechanistic basis for G418-induced PTC readthrough [
77
,
78
], remains incompletely understood. The sequence surrounding the
BRCA2
PTC, GU
UAG
AC, is not particularly prone to readthrough [
47
,
79
]. Moreover, the present analysis has ruled out mutations or quantitative alterations in tyrosine tRNAs. While modifications of tRNAs (reviewed in [
80
]) have been observed in the ABT
R
clones, none of these appear to be responsible for the observed readthrough (
Supplementary Table S3
and footnotes). In particular, increased incorporation of inosine, a base that increases alternative translation when present at tRNA residue 34 [
81
,
82
], is found in the ABT
R
clones, but inosine does not bind G (the third base of the UAG codon that is translated to Tyr in these cells) [
83
,
84
], seemingly ruling out a role for this modification in the readthrough. Likewise, pseudouridine in the anticodon can suppress PTCs through noncanonical base pairing [
85
,
86
], but increased pseudouridine is only detected in two of the four ABT
R
clones (
Supplementary Table S3
) and occurs in the absence of a significant increase in pseudouridine synthase at the mRNA level (Fig.
4C
). Additional considerations argue against the possibility that other modifications shown in
Supplementary Table S3
contribute to readthrough in all four clones, but we cannot rule out the possibility that (i) other tRNA modifications not measured in this study contribute to the readthrough, (ii) different modifications contribute to the readthrough in different ABT
R
clones, or (iii) modifications at the level of the mRNA or rRNA contribute to the readthrough [
87
,
88
]. Likewise, the present transcriptomic and proteomic analyses argue against large changes in one or two individual components of the translation termination machinery. However, we cannot rule out the possibility that a posttranslational modification of one or a few key proteins not measured in the present study contributes to the observed readthrough phenotype. Alternatively, because the resistant clones harbor multiple small changes that have been reported to contribute to increased translational readthrough in other contexts, including decreased expression of the termination protein ETF1 and increased EEF1A (Fig.
4
and
Supplementary Fig. S6
), it is also possible that multiple changes in the termination machinery, each <2-fold in magnitude, might combinatorially result in the observed translational readthrough.
Second, factors that contribute to the codon specificity of the readthrough are unclear. Results in Fig.
5C
and D and
Supplementary Fig. S8A
and
E
indicate that ABT
R
clones are more likely to read through UAG than other stop codons. While this might indicate the presence of an RNA or protein modification that specifically enhances recognition of the UAG codon by a tyrosine tRNA that ordinarily decodes UAU or UAC, the preferential incorporation of tyrosine at the PTCs (
Supplementary Table S2A
, Fig.
5B
and D) might also reflect the fact that tyrosine tRNA facilely enhances readthrough when sequences are near-cognate [
89
] or tRNA levels are high [
54
].
Third, the cause of the increased BRCA2 mRNA in the ABT
R
clones (Fig.
4A
) is incompletely understood and could be due to changes in NMD. While transcriptomic and proteomic analyses in Fig.
4
and
Supplementary Fig. S6
argue against large changes in one or two NMD proteins, decreased levels of SMG7, SMG8, and DPC2 observed in the ABTR clones could potentially result in the trend toward diminished NMD, as suggested by results in Fig.
4B
. Alternatively, it has been reported that NMD can be diminished as a consequence of the readthrough process itself. In particular, increased readthrough induced by downregulation of the ribosome recycling factor ABCE1 reportedly inhibits NMD and increases levels of NMD-sensitive messages [
90
]. While ABCE1 was not appreciably altered in the present study, it is nonetheless possible that the readthrough process detected in the ABT
R
clones altered binding and degradation of the BRCA2 message by the NMD machinery. Finally, we cannot at present rule out the possibility that the elevated BRCA2 mRNA instead reflects enhanced transcription. Whatever the explanation, the increased BRCA2 mRNA provides an opportunity for an inefficient readthrough process to generate small but detectable amounts of BRCA2 protein with restitution of WT protein sequence (Fig.
5B
).
Fourth, it is unclear whether the present results are unique to selection with the PARPi veliparib. Although veliparib was initially reported to trap PARP1 and PARP2 on DNA less efficiently than other PARPis [
39
], subsequent studies have indicated that veliparib is similar to niraparib and rucaparib in its PARP trapping ability [
91
,
92
], appearing to rule out a unique property of veliparib as a PARPi. Moreover, the resulting cells are equally resistant to four additional PARPis, indicating that the resistance is not unique to veliparib.
Finally, it is unclear whether readthrough occurs in the clinical setting. Comprehensive analyses have failed to find an explanation for PARPi resistance in a large fraction of ovarian cancers exhibiting PARPi resistance in the clinic [
93–95
]. While further studies are required to determine whether lapses in translational fidelity contribute to this resistance, several limitations to current technology make these studies difficult. Immunohistochemical methods could in principle be used to search for BRCA2 expression in cancers that are PARPi resistant but retain fully penetrant nonsense mutations. Unfortunately, this approach requires validated, high-quality antibodies that detect C-terminal BRCA2 epitopes at the low levels observed in ABT
R
clones, and these reagents are not currently available. Alternatively, BRCA2 can be immunoprecipitated and detected by mass spectrometry (e.g. Fig.
3F
and
Supplementary Fig. S5D
). However, large amounts of material are needed due to the low abundance of BRCA2, and the presence of normal
BRCA2-
WT stromal cells (e.g. lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells) will confound any analysis involving tumor homogenates. A hybrid approach in which tumor cells are isolated by laser capture microdissection and subjected to immunoprecipitation-MS/MS is appealing but currently lacks the sensitivity to detect a low abundance protein like BRCA2.
While the protein mass spectrometry played a key role in the identification of PTC readthrough as a mechanism of chemotherapy resistance, it is important to emphasize that typical mass spectrometry analyses of cancer cell lines and clinical samples would miss the readthrough results reported here. As illustrated in the present work, detection of readthrough products requires specialized database searches to identify peptides where an amino acid is incorporated at a stop codon by the cellular translation machinery. As a result, further investigation with appropriate search methods will be needed to determine whether stop codon readthrough is observed more widely or is limited to the cell line described in this study.
